line.statement: A `//` token starts a comment that runs to the end of the same line; the comment, including its delimiter, is ignored.
line.outputs: zero tokens; the remainder of the line is not lexed.

block.statement: A `/*` token starts a comment terminated by the first (next) `*/`; comments do not nest, and the comment with its delimiters is ignored.
block.formal: `/*` … `*/` ⇒ no token; the first `*/` after `/*` terminates the comment (no nesting).
block.outputs: zero tokens up to and including the first terminating `*/`.

placement.statement: A comment may appear anywhere whitespace may appear and is ignored, i.e. it is whitespace for the purpose of token separation.
placement.formal: comment ≡ whitespace in the token stream.
placement.inputs: a token stream; a comment occurrence.
placement.outputs: the token stream with the comment elided as if whitespace.

default-type.statement: An unsuffixed integer literal has type `i32` when no context type applies.
default-type.formal: `type(lit) = i32` if `ctx_int = ⊥` (not at a context position of integer type).
default-type.inputs: an unsuffixed integer literal; absence of an integer context type.

context-type.statement: An unsuffixed integer literal takes the context's integer type when one is present at a context position.
context-type.formal: `type(lit) = ctx_int` if `ctx_int ≠ ⊥`; `ctx_int` is the expected type at a context position, per `type.context.positions` and `type.context.propagation`.
context-type.inputs: an unsuffixed integer literal; an integer context type.
context-type.outputs: the literal typed as the context type.

radix.statement: Integer literals are decimal, hexadecimal (`0x…`), or binary (`0b…`). There is no octal form and no type suffix on any literal.
radix.formal: `digits ::= dec | '0x' hex+ | '0b' bin+`; `literal ::= digits` (no suffix grammar).
radix.outputs: its value in the declared radix; a suffix is a lexical error.

range.statement: An integer literal must be representable in its resolved type (default or context); an out-of-range literal is a compile error.
range.formal: `lit` valid iff `value(lit) ∈ range(type(lit))`, else `err`. No wrapping is applied at the lexical/typing stage.
range.inputs: an integer literal and its resolved type (per `lexical.integer.default-type`/`lexical.integer.context-type`).
range.outputs: `err` if the value does not fit; otherwise the typed value.

min-literal.statement: A unary `-` applied to an integer literal whose value is exactly `2^(N-1)` (out of range for a signed context type of width `N`) folds to the minimum signed value, so `-2147483648` writes `i32::MIN`.
min-literal.formal: `-lit` where `⟦lit⟧ = 2^(N-1)` and the context is a signed integer of width `N` ⇒ `-2^(N-1)` (the minimum value), despite the literal itself being out of range.
min-literal.inputs: `-lit` with `lit = 2^(N-1)` in a signed context of width `N`.
min-literal.outputs: the minimum value of the signed type.
min-literal.notes: applies to any radix (`-2147483648`, `-0x80000000`, `-0b100…0`); only when the literal is exactly the boundary magnitude.

default-type.statement: An unsuffixed float literal has type `f32` when no context type applies.
default-type.formal: `type(lit) = f32` if `ctx_float = ⊥` (not at a context position of float type).
default-type.inputs: an unsuffixed float literal; absence of a float context type.

context-type.statement: An unsuffixed float literal takes the context's float type when one is present at a context position.
context-type.formal: `type(lit) = ctx_float` if `ctx_float ≠ ⊥`; `ctx_float` is the expected type at a context position, per `type.context.positions` and `type.context.propagation`.
context-type.inputs: an unsuffixed float literal; a float context type.
context-type.outputs: the literal typed as the context type.

form.statement: A float literal is decimal and must contain a `.` or an exponent; digits are required on the right of any `.` (so `1.` is illegal, `.5` is legal). `1.0`, `.5`, `1e10`, `1.5e-3` are legal; a bare integer is not a float; there is no hex float.
form.formal: `float ::= digits+ exp | digits* '.' digits+ [exp]`, where `exp ::= [eE] [+-]? digits+`. `1.0`, `.5`, `1e10`, `1.5e-3` ✓; `1.` ⇒ `err`; `1` ⇒ integer (not float).

rounding.statement: A float literal is rounded to its resolved type per IEEE 754 round-to-nearest; overflow yields ±infinity and underflow yields subnormal/±0. This is never an error.
rounding.formal: `value(lit) = round_T(lit)` with IEEE 754 round-to-nearest (tie-breaking per `type.float.ieee`); `|lit| > max(T)` ⇒ `±inf`; subnormal results are allowed. No diagnostic is produced.
rounding.inputs: a float literal and its resolved type `T`.
rounding.outputs: the nearest representable value in `T` (possibly `±inf`, `±0`, or subnormal); never `err`.

special-literal.statement: `inf` and `nan` are keywords that denote the special float values `+∞` and NaN, context-typed like float literals: `f32` by default, or the context's float type. `-inf` (unary minus) denotes `-∞`.
special-literal.outputs: the corresponding special float value, context-typed.
special-literal.notes: `inf`/`nan` may be used to write these values and to compare `x == inf`/`x == -inf`; they cannot detect NaN (see `type.float.nan-test`).

separator.statement: `_` is a digit separator in any numeric literal (integer or float); it is valid only where a digit valid in the literal's radix appears on both its immediate left and right, and it never affects the value.
separator.formal: `_` valid iff a digit (valid in the literal's radix) is immediately to its left and to its right; else `err`. `value(…a_b…) = value(…ab…)`. `_1`, `1_`, `1__0`, `2__2`, `0x_FF`, `0b_1`, `1000_.2` ⇒ `err`; `1_000`, `1_000.5`, `1_0_0_0.5`, `0xF_F` ⇒ valid.
separator.outputs: the value with `_` elided; a misplaced `_` ⇒ `err`.

set.statement: The keyword set is exactly: `let mut fn struct enum match switch if else while for in yield break continue return as true false undefined inf nan`.
set.formal: `KW = { let, mut, fn, struct, enum, match, switch, if, else, while, for, in, yield, break, continue, return, as, true, false, undefined, inf, nan }`. A keyword is never a valid identifier.

reservation.statement: The primitive type names — `bool i8 i16 i32 i64 u8 u16 u32 u64 usz isz f32 f64 byte` — are reserved and cannot be shadowed; they are not keywords, but type names resolved like any other type.
reservation.formal: `shadow(name) = err` for `name ∈ PTN`; `PTN = {bool, i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, usz, isz, f32, f64, byte}`.
reservation.inputs: a declaration attempting to bind/declare a name.

order.formal: total order (given) over the operator set; a binary op's operands are parsed at the next-tighter level.
order.outputs: its parse tree consistent with the precedence order.

bitwise-vs-relational.statement: Bitwise operators bind tighter than comparisons: `a & b == 0` parses as `(a & b) == 0`.
bitwise-vs-relational.inputs: an expression mixing bitwise and relational operators.
bitwise-vs-relational.outputs: bitwise applied to its operands before the comparison.

semantics.statement: Each compound assignment `x op= rhs` means `x = x op rhs` (semantic desugaring) and, like `=`, is a statement; `x` is evaluated once — its address is computed once and its value read once, then written.
semantics.formal: `x op= rhs ⇒ x = x op rhs` (semantic, not textual); `x` is evaluated once (address + read once, then one write). Result category = statement.
semantics.outputs: the desugared assignment with `x` evaluated once; no value produced.
semantics.notes: textual desugaring (two evaluations of `x`) is rejected as dangerous and hard to reason about; `a[i()] += 1` calls `i()` once.

set.statement: The primitive types are exactly `bool i8 i16 i32 i64 u8 u16 u32 u64 usz isz f32 f64 byte`.
set.formal: `PT = {bool, i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32, u64, usz, isz, f32, f64, byte}`.

size-align.statement: Primitive sizes and alignments, in bytes: `i8`/`u8`/`byte`/`bool` = 1; `i16`/`u16` = 2; `i32`/`u32`/`f32` = 4; `i64`/`u64`/`f64` = 8; `usz`/`isz` = the target's native word size (8 on the 64-bit baseline). A primitive's alignment equals its size.
size-align.formal: `size(T) = align(T)` for `T ∈ PT`, with the table: `{1: i8,u8,byte,bool; 2: i16,u16; 4: i32,u32,f32; 8: i64,u64,f64,usz,isz}`.

no-implicit-conversion.statement: No primitive type converts to another implicitly.
no-implicit-conversion.formal: For `e : T` used where `S` is expected and `T ≠ S`, the program is rejected unless an explicit `as` is present.
no-implicit-conversion.inputs: an expression of primitive type `T` in a position expecting `S ≠ T`.
no-implicit-conversion.outputs: no implicit conversion is applied; the compiler never inserts one.

ops.statement: `bool` supports logical (`&& || !`) and comparison (`== != < <= > >=`) operators, and no arithmetic.
ops.outputs: allowed iff in the set; else `err`.

representation.statement: `bool` has a canonical representation: `false` = `0x00` and `true` = `0x01`; reading a `bool` holding any other bit pattern is undefined behavior.
representation.formal: `false ≡ 0x00`, `true ≡ 0x01`; a `bool` load whose byte is not `0x00`/`0x01` ⇒ `unspecified`.
representation.outputs: `false`/`true` for canonical values; `unspecified` for a non-canonical byte.

ops.statement: All integer types (`i*`, `u*`, `isz`, `usz`) support the full arithmetic set, including shifts `<<`/`>>`.
ops.inputs: an operator applied to integer operands.
ops.notes: shift semantics and out-of-range behavior are `expression.shift.semantics`, `expression.shift.constant-out-of-bounds`, `expression.shift.out-of-bounds`.

overflow.statement: Integer arithmetic wraps on overflow (two's complement); overflow is neither an error nor undefined behavior.
overflow.formal: `a ⊕ b ≡ (a ⊕ b) mod 2^N` (for width N), i.e. two's-complement wrap, for all integer ops.
overflow.inputs: an integer operation whose mathematical result exceeds the width.

division-modulo-by-zero.statement: Division and modulo by zero are undefined behavior; no check is emitted.
division-modulo-by-zero.inputs: integer division or modulo with zero divisor.

signed-division-truncate.statement: Signed division and modulo truncate toward zero: `-7 / 2 == -3`, `-7 % 2 == -1`.
signed-division-truncate.formal: `a / b = trunc(a / b)`; `a % b = a − trunc(a / b)·b` (sign of result follows `a`).
signed-division-truncate.inputs: signed integer division or modulo with nonzero divisor.

signed-division-overflow.statement: The `INT_MIN / -1` and `INT_MIN % -1` overflow cases are undefined behavior, matching C.
signed-division-overflow.inputs: signed division/modulo of the minimum value by −1.

ops.statement: `f32`/`f64` support the full arithmetic set except `%`.
ops.inputs: an operator applied to float operands.

ieee.statement: Floating-point arithmetic is fully IEEE 754 conformant: round-half-to-even, no FMA contraction, subnormals supported (no flush-to-zero), quiet NaN propagation, and no fast-math relaxations.
ieee.formal: each float operation is independently rounded to nearest with ties-to-even (IEEE 754 default); no `fast-math`, no FMA contraction; subnormals preserved; NaN is quiet-propagating.
ieee.outputs: the IEEE 754 correctly-rounded result, with no contraction or flush.

nan.statement: NaN compares unequal to everything, including itself: `NaN == NaN` is `false`.
nan.formal: for NaN `q`: `q == v` is `false` ∀v (including `v = q`); `q != v` is `true`.

nan-order.statement: NaN is *unordered* in ordering comparisons per IEEE 754: `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` with any NaN operand all evaluate to `false`.
nan-order.formal: for NaN `q`: `q < x`, `q <= x`, `q > x`, `q >= x`, `x < q`, `x <= q`, `x > q`, `x >= q` ⇒ `false` for all `x`.

nan-test.statement: `x != x` (equivalently `!(x == x)`) is the canonical NaN test: it is `true` iff `x` is NaN. `x == x` is `true` iff `x` is not NaN (a real number).
nan-test.formal: `x != x ⇔ x is NaN`; `x == x ⇔ x is not NaN`.

special-arith.statement: Arithmetic on the special values `±inf` and NaN follows IEEE 754, stated explicitly: `+inf + +inf = +inf`; `+inf + -inf = NaN`; `inf - inf = NaN`; `±inf * 0 = NaN`; `±inf * ±x = ±inf` for `x ≠ 0`; `x / ±inf = ±0` for finite `x`; `±inf / ±inf = NaN`; `±inf / ±x = ±inf` for finite `x`; and any operation with a NaN operand yields NaN.
special-arith.formal: the enumerated IEEE special-value results above; signs combine per IEEE (sign of a product/quotient is the xor of operand signs).
special-arith.inputs: a float `+`/`-`/`*`/`/` with `±inf` or NaN operands.

nan-kind.statement: Spite produces and propagates quiet NaN only; signaling NaN is not a language concept, and the NaN payload (mantissa bits) is unspecified.
nan-kind.formal: every NaN-producing operation yields qNaN; no operation produces sNaN; the NaN payload bits are `unspecified`.
nan-kind.inputs: any float operation that yields NaN.
nan-kind.outputs: a quiet NaN with an unspecified payload.

no-flags.statement: Float operations raise no traps and maintain no sticky exception flags; the resulting value is the complete observable effect.
no-flags.formal: an FP operation's only observable effect is its result value (`±inf`/NaN/subnormal); no exception trap or flag is produced or exposed.
no-flags.outputs: the IEEE value, with no trap or flag side effect.

signed-zero.statement: Signed zero follows IEEE 754: `-0.0 == 0.0` is `true`, and `-0.0` is distinguishable (e.g. `1.0 / -0.0` is `-inf`; the sign is observable).

division-by-zero.statement: Float division by zero follows IEEE 754: `x / 0.0` yields `±inf` (sign per operands) and `0.0 / 0.0` yields NaN; it is defined behavior, not UB.
division-by-zero.inputs: a float division with a zero divisor.

modulo.statement: `%` is defined on integer operands only; `f32 % f32` and `f64 % f64` are compile errors.
modulo.formal: `a % b` valid iff `type(a), type(b)` are integers; float operands ⇒ `err`.

domain.statement: `byte` is one unit of opaque, unmarked data over the full 0–255 range — not a number and not necessarily text.
domain.outputs: a value in `[0,255]` with no numeric semantics beyond ordering/equality.

ops.statement: `byte` supports equality/ordering (`== != < <= > >=`) and bitwise (`& | ^ ~`), and no arithmetic or shifts (shifts are integer-only). Ordering compares the byte's 8-bit value as an unsigned integer in `0..=255`; equality is bitwise.
ops.outputs: allowed iff in the set; ordering/equality per unsigned `0..=255` value.

escapes.statement: A `byte` literal supports the escapes `\0 \n \r \t \\ \" \'` (all ASCII control/quote characters).
escapes.outputs: its byte value after escape resolution.

ascii.statement: The non-escaped `'x'` form is a single 1-byte codepoint — ASCII (0–127); a multi-byte codepoint like `'é'` is a compile error.
ascii.formal: `'c'` (unescaped) valid iff `0x00 ≤ c ≤ 0x7F`, else `err`. Above-ASCII bytes are written as `0bXXXXXXXX` bit patterns.
ascii.inputs: a `byte` literal using the non-escaped form.
ascii.outputs: `err` if the source character is not ASCII.

bits.statement: A `byte` may be initialized from a binary `0bXXXXXXXX` or hex `0xNN` integer literal (a raw bit pattern), via context typing; the value must fit in 0–255.
bits.formal: `let b: byte = 0bXXXXXXXX` / `0xNN` ⇒ `b = ⟦lit⟧` (context-typed to `byte`); the value must be in `[0, 255]`, else `err`.
bits.inputs: a binary/hex literal in a `byte` context.
bits.outputs: the byte with that bit pattern.

positions.statement: The positions that establish an expected (context) type are exactly: a binding's type annotation, a parameter's type, a return type, a struct field's type, an array element type, a match/switch arm's unified result type, a subscript index (`usz`), and a range endpoint (`usz`). The target of `as` is *not* a context position.
positions.formal: `ctx_positions = { binding, parameter, return, struct-field, array-element, match/switch-arm, subscript-index(usz), range-endpoint(usz) }`; `as`-target ∉ `ctx_positions`.
positions.inputs: a syntactic site carrying a type expectation.
positions.outputs: whether that site is a context position.

propagation.statement: A context type propagates bidirectionally into the entire expression occupying the position, including its subexpressions (literals and operator operands); the scope is tightly bounded to that expression and does not extend beyond it.
propagation.formal: if `E` occupies a context position of type `T`, then `E` and all its subexpressions are checked against `T`. E.g. `let d: u8 = 1 + 2` types `1`, `2`, and `+` as `u8`.
propagation.inputs: a context position of type `T` and the expression `E` in it.

conflict.statement: When two subexpressions carry incompatible types in a position requiring one type (e.g. binary operator operands of different types) and no coercion applies, it is a compile error; the compiler never auto-resolves the conflict.
conflict.formal: `a ⊕ b` with `type(a) ≠ type(b)` and no coercible direction ⇒ `err`.
conflict.inputs: a binary operator (or analogous position) with two differently-typed operands.

nested-view.statement: A slice `T[]` or fixed array `T[n]` may have an element type `T` that is itself a slice or a reference — e.g. `byte[][]` (a slice of `byte[]`), `byte[][n]` (an array of `byte[]`), `&T[]` (a slice of `&T`). There is no arbitrary depth limit. The single prohibited nesting is `&&T` (reference to reference).
nested-view.formal: `T` in `T[]` / `T[n]` is unrestricted — a value, slice, or reference, to any depth; `&&T` is the one exception (`err`).
nested-view.inputs: a slice or array type with a slice/reference element.

converts.statement: `as` converts between primitive types in either direction (widening or narrowing).
converts.formal: `x as T` valid for `type(x) ∈ PT`, `T ∈ PT`, `type(x) ≠ T` (subject to the exclusions in `expression.cast.no-struct`/`no-reinterpret`/`bool`); yields a value of type `T`.
converts.inputs: `x as T` with primitive source and target.
converts.outputs: a value of type `T`, per `expression.cast.float-integer` (float↔int) and other `expression.cast.*` rules.

narrow-warning.statement: A lossy cast — one whose target type cannot represent every value of the source type — produces a compiler warning.
narrow-warning.formal: `warn(x as T) ⇔ lossy(type(x), T)`, where `lossy(S, T) ⇔ ∃ v ∈ S: (v as T) as S ≠ v`. Lossy cases: width-shrink (any sign), signed↔unsigned same-width, int→float (precision), float→int (truncation). Non-lossy: widening int/float, `byte`↔`u8`.
narrow-warning.outputs: a warning diagnostic (not an error) iff the cast is lossy.

no-struct.statement: `as` does not apply to structs; there is no struct-to-struct conversion.
no-struct.formal: `x as T` with `type(x)` or `T` a struct ⇒ `err`.
no-struct.inputs: a cast involving a struct type.

no-reinterpret.statement: Bit-level reinterpretation (e.g. `f32` raw bits as `u32`) and extracting an enum variant's tag are not part of `as`.
no-reinterpret.formal: reinterpretation/tag-extraction have no `as` form; attempting them ⇒ `err` (no such operation in this phase).
no-reinterpret.inputs: an attempt to reinterpret bits or extract a tag via `as`.

bool.statement: `as` to or from `bool` is a compile error.
bool.inputs: a cast with `bool` as source or target.

byte-u8.statement: `as` between `byte` and `u8` is allowed in either direction.
byte-u8.formal: `byte as u8` and `u8 as byte` are valid; value preserved (both are 0–255).

float-integer.statement: int→float rounds to nearest (ties-to-even, IEEE-conformant); float→int truncates toward zero; a float→int cast whose source is NaN or out of the target's range yields `0`.
float-integer.formal: `i as f = round_nearest_even(f, i)`; `f as i = trunc_toward_zero(f)` when `f` is finite and `trunc_toward_zero(f) ∈ [min(i), max(i)]`, else `0`; `NaN as i = 0`; `±inf as i = 0`.
float-integer.outputs: the converted value; `0` for NaN/±inf/out-of-range float→int.
float-integer.notes: out-of-range/NaN → `0` is deliberate (the "closest concept to unspecified" on an integer); it is fully deterministic, not UB.

operand-typing.statement: The operand of `as` is typed independently of the cast target; a literal operand takes its default width (`i32`/`f32`), and the cast then converts that value to the target type.
operand-typing.formal: `E as T` ⇒ first resolve `type(E)` (a literal ⇒ default `i32`/`f32`, never `T`), then convert the value to `T`. `300 as u8` ⇒ `300 : i32` truncated to `u8`.
operand-typing.outputs: the operand typed independently, then converted to the target.

constant-expression.statement: A compile-time constant expression is a closed expression over literals (int/float/byte) and the operators applicable to those literal types, constant-folded; it contains no function calls and no reads of non-literal bindings.
constant-expression.formal: `const-expr ::= literal | unop const-expr | const-expr binop const-expr`, where `unop`/`binop` are the operators defined for the literal's type; no `fn` calls, no binding references. Folded to a value at compile time.
constant-expression.outputs: whether it is a constant; if so, its folded value.
constant-expression.notes: a future `const`/comptime facility (not yet in the reference) may extend this domain; the reference currently has no `const` keyword or const-bindings.

eval-order.statement: Sub-expressions are evaluated in source order, left-to-right: binary operands, function arguments, and subscript base-then-index all evaluate deterministically left-to-right.
eval-order.formal: for `E₁ ⊕ E₂`, `⟦E₁⟧` evaluates before `⟦E₂⟧`; for `f(a₁,…,aₙ)`, `aᵢ` evaluates before `aᵢ₊₁`; for `a[i]`, `a` evaluates before `i`.
eval-order.notes: deliberately not C's "unspecified" order; source order is the defined evaluation order.

short-circuit.statement: `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right operand is evaluated only if the left operand does not already determine the result.
short-circuit.formal: `a && b` evaluates `b` only if `⟦a⟧ = true`; `a || b` evaluates `b` only if `⟦a⟧ = false`; otherwise `b` is not evaluated.

target-lvalue.statement: The target of `=` and compound assignment must be an l-value — a binding, `*r`, `s.f`, or `a[i]`; assigning to a literal, a call result, or any r-value is a compile error.
target-lvalue.formal: `lhs = rhs` / `lhs op= rhs` valid iff `lhs` is an l-value; else `err`.
target-lvalue.outputs: `err` if the target is not an l-value.

semantics.statement: `x << n` shifts `x` left `n` bits (zero-fill). `x >> n` shifts `x` right `n` bits: arithmetic (sign-extending) for a signed integer (`i*`, `isz`), logical (zero-fill) for an unsigned integer (`u*`, `usz`).
semantics.formal: `<<` zero-fills on the right; `>>` sign-fills on the left when `type(x)` is signed, zero-fills when unsigned.

constant-out-of-bounds.statement: A shift by a compile-time constant amount that is negative or ≥ the operand's bit width is a compile error.
constant-out-of-bounds.formal: `x << n` / `x >> n` where `n` is a constant expression (`expression.constant-expression`) and `n < 0` or `n ≥ width(type(x))` ⇒ `err`.
constant-out-of-bounds.inputs: a shift with a constant out-of-range amount.

out-of-bounds.statement: A shift by a runtime amount that is negative or ≥ the operand's bit width is undefined behavior; no check is emitted.
out-of-bounds.formal: `x << n` / `x >> n` where `n` is a runtime value and `n < 0` or `n ≥ width(type(x))` ⇒ `unspecified`.
out-of-bounds.inputs: a shift with a runtime out-of-range amount.

let.statement: `let` declares a constant l-value: the binding cannot be reassigned after initialization.
let.formal: `let x: T …` ⇒ `x` is an l-value of type `T`; `x = …` after init ⇒ `err`.
let.inputs: a `let` binding and any subsequent reassignment.
let.outputs: the binding is immutable; reassignment is `err`.

mutable.statement: `mut` declares a mutable l-value: the binding can be reassigned, and its value and fields/elements are writable.
mutable.formal: `mut x: T …` ⇒ `x` is a reassignable l-value of type `T`; field/element writes are permitted.
mutable.outputs: reassignment and field/element writes are permitted.

field-write.statement: A binding's mutability is transitive (deep) over a value type: writing a field of a struct value or an element of an array value through a `let` binding (`s.f = v`, `a[i] = v`, and their compound-assign forms) is a compile error. View types (references, slices) are unaffected — their writability is carried by the view type, not the binding (§3.2, §4.2).
field-write.formal: for a value-type binding `s`/`a`, `s.f = v` / `a[i] = v` valid iff `binding(s)`/`binding(a)` = `mut`, else `err`.
field-write.inputs: a field/element write through a value-type binding.
field-write.outputs: `err` if the enclosing binding is not `mut`.

no-type-no-initialization.statement: A binding must have either a type annotation or an initializer (from which the type is inferred); a binding with neither is a compile error.
no-type-no-initialization.formal: `let x;` / `mut x;` with no type annotation and no initializer ⇒ `err`.
no-type-no-initialization.inputs: a binding with no type and no initializer.

block.statement: Bindings are scoped to their enclosing block.
block.formal: a binding is visible from its declaration to the end of the innermost enclosing `{ }`; not outside it.
block.outputs: whether the use is in scope.

shadow.statement: An inner binding may shadow an outer binding of the same name.
shadow.formal: a name bound in an inner scope hides the outer binding within that inner scope; resolution inside the inner scope finds the innermost binding.
shadow.inputs: two bindings of the same name in nested scopes.
shadow.outputs: the inner binding is resolved within its scope.

redeclaration.statement: A name may be bound at most once per scope; redeclaring the same name in the same block is a compile error. Only a nested scope may shadow.
redeclaration.formal: two bindings of the same name in the same scope ⇒ `err`; shadowing is legal only across a scope boundary (a nested block).
redeclaration.inputs: two same-name bindings in one scope.

defaulted.formal: binding with a type and no initializer ⇒ form (a).
defaulted.inputs: a binding with type, no initializer.

undefined.statement: `= undefined` explicitly leaves the value uninitialized.
undefined.formal: `= undefined` ⇒ form (b); legal only for value types (see `variable.initialization.undefined.value-type`).

brace.statement: `= T{ .field = v, … }` brace-initializes a value, listing a subset of fields.

semantics.statement: Default-initialization sets each field to its declared default where one exists, else to the all-zero-bits value of its type (recursively).
semantics.formal: `init(x) = ⟨ default(f) if declared, else zero(type(f)) ⟩` over every field/element. `zero(i*/u*) = 0`; `zero(bool) = false` (0x00); `zero(f*) = +0.0`; `zero(byte) = 0x00`; `zero(T[n])` = each element `zero(T)`; `zero(S)` = each field recursively.
semantics.outputs: the value with each field defaulted or all-zero-bits.

semantics.statement: `undefined` leaves the value as garbage — whatever bits were already there.
semantics.formal: `undefined` ⇒ no store; the value is the prior contents of the storage.

value-type.statement: `undefined` is legal only for a value type — a type whose layout, transitively, contains no reference and no slice.
value-type.formal: `undefined` valid iff `is_value_type(T)`, where `is_value_type(T) = ¬ contains_ref_or_slice(T)` (transitive over fields and array elements).
value-type.outputs: `err` if `T` transitively contains a reference or slice.

semantics.statement: Brace-init zeroes/applies defaults to all fields except those explicitly listed, which take the given values.
semantics.formal: `T{ .fᵢ = vᵢ }` ⇒ `fᵢ = vᵢ` for listed fields; all other fields = `default`/`zero` as in `variable.initialization.defaulted.semantics`.
semantics.outputs: listed fields set; unlisted fields zeroed/defaulted.

reference-field.statement: A struct with a reference-typed field cannot use form (a); form (c) must supply every reference field explicitly.
reference-field.formal: if `∃ f ∈ fields(S): type(f) ∈ ref`, then form (a) ⇒ `err`; form (c) must list every such `f`.
reference-field.inputs: a defaulted or brace-init of a struct with reference fields.
reference-field.outputs: `err` for form (a); `err` for form (c) omitting a reference field.

type-inference.statement: `let t = expr;` infers `t`'s type bottom-up from `expr`: `type(t) = type(expr)`, equivalent to writing the type explicitly.
type-inference.formal: `type(t) = type(expr)` computed bottom-up; a literal initializer takes its default width (`i32`/`f32`) since no annotation supplies a context. No outer expected type flows into an un-annotated initializer.
type-inference.inputs: a binding with an initializer and no type annotation.
type-inference.outputs: the binding typed as the initializer's type.

representation.statement: A reference `&T` is a non-nullable indirection to a value — one machine word (a pointer).
representation.formal: `size(&T) = size(&mut T) = 8` (one machine word, 64-bit); the stored value is an address.
representation.outputs: its representation as a pointer-sized value.

guarantee.outputs: a non-null pointer to a live value.
guarantee.statement: A `&T` is never null and is always bound to a live value at the moment it is created.
guarantee.formal: at creation, `⟦&x⟧ ≠ null` and points to a live value; no syntax produces null; `undefined` cannot initialize a reference or reference-holding value.

scope.statement: The non-null guarantee is about creation, not the referent's lifetime: a reference may outlive its referent and dangle, which is unchecked.
scope.formal: the guarantee holds only at the creation site; lifetime is governed by `reference.dangling.footgun`.

type-vs-op.statement: `&`/`&mut` before a type form reference types; before an l-value they take an address (yielding `&T`/`&mut T`, or a slice for an array-like l-value); between two operands `&` is bitwise AND.
type-vs-op.formal: context-disambiguation: type position ⇒ reference type; unary on l-value ⇒ address/slice; binary ⇒ bitwise AND.

split.statement: `&T` is a read-only view; `&mut T` grants write access to the referent.
split.inputs: a reference type and a write attempt.

take-constraint.statement: Taking `&mut` of a value requires that value's own binding to be `mut`; for a field or array element (a value-type sub-value), it requires the *enclosing* binding to be `mut` (`&mut s.f`, `&mut a[i]` need `s`/`a` to be `mut`). The same holds for `&mut` on an array-like l-value.
take-constraint.formal: `&mut x` valid iff `binding(x) = mut`, else `err`; for a value-type field/element, `&mut s.f` / `&mut a[i]` valid iff `binding(s)`/`binding(a)` = `mut`, else `err`.
take-constraint.inputs: a `&mut`-taking of an l-value (binding, field, or element).
take-constraint.outputs: `err` if the owning binding is not `mut`.

lvalue.statement: `&e` / `&mut e` requires `e` to be an l-value; taking the address of a temporary, a literal, or a call result is a compile error.
lvalue.formal: `&e`/`&mut e` valid iff `e` is an l-value (a binding, or a dereference/projection naming storage); else `err`. `&(x+1)`, `&10`, `&foo()` ⇒ `err`.

explicit.statement: Access through a reference is explicit: `*` dereferences to the whole referent; `->` dereferences for member access.
explicit.inputs: a reference and a dereference/arrow expression.

write-requires-mutable.statement: Writing through `*` requires `&mut`; `*` on a `&T` reads but cannot write.

rebind.statement: `=` on a reference variable rebinds it to a new address; it never writes through.
rebind.formal: `r = e` (where `r : &T`/`&mut T`) assigns `e`'s address to `r`; the referent is unaffected.
rebind.inputs: an assignment to a reference variable.

statement.statement: `=` is a statement, not an expression: it produces no value and may not appear where a value is expected.
statement.formal: `=` yields no value; result category = statement.

type-match.statement: The right-hand side of a rebind must match the reference's type and mutability: a `&mut u64` is assigned a `&mut u64`, never a `&u64`.
type-match.formal: `r = e` valid iff `type(e) = type(r)` (including mutability); `&u64 → &mut u64` ⇒ `err`.

dot.statement: `.` accesses a member at the receiver's own indirection level.
dot.formal: `r.f` on a reference projects the reference to the field (a reference of the same mutability); `p.f` on a value gives the member l-value.
dot.outputs: a field reference (on a reference) or field l-value (on a value).

arrow.statement: `->` dereferences one level and then accesses the member; it is meaningful only on a reference and always gives the member value.
arrow.outputs: the member value after one dereference.

projection.statement: On a value, `.` gives the member value itself; on a reference, `.` gives a reference to the member of the same mutability (`r.x` on `&mut Point` is `&mut f32`).
projection.formal: `type(p.f) = type(f)` (l-value); `type(r.f) = &mut type(f)` if `r : &mut Point`, `& type(f)` if `r : &Point`.
projection.inputs: a `.` access on a value vs. a reference.
projection.outputs: the member value vs. the projected reference.

rebind.statement: Compound assignment (`+=`, …) is defined as `x = x op rhs`, so it rebinds a reference rather than writing through it; to write through, dereference first (`*d += 1`).
rebind.formal: `d += rhs` (on `d : &T`) ⇒ `d = d + rhs` — an error, since an address has no arithmetic; `*d += rhs` writes through.
rebind.inputs: a compound assignment to a reference.

no-default.statement: A reference-typed field cannot declare a default value.
no-default.inputs: a struct field declaration with a default on a reference type.

initialization-required.statement: A struct with a reference-typed field requires full brace-init supplying a real referent for each reference field; form (a) and form (b) are both errors.
initialization-required.formal: for `S` with a reference field: form (a) ⇒ `err` (no default), form (b) ⇒ `err` (not a value type), form (c) must list each reference field.
initialization-required.inputs: initialization of a struct with reference fields.

constraint.statement: A function may not directly `return &local;` or `return &mut local;` where `local` is owned by that function's own stack frame.
constraint.inputs: a return of an address-of a frame-owned local.

scope.statement: The `return &local` constraint covers only frame-owned locals; returning a reference to a referent not owned by the frame (e.g. a `&mut` parameter's referent) is legal. The language currently defines no global variables, so a global referent is not a concept.
scope.formal: `return &x` valid iff `x` is not a frame-owned local; `return &mut *p` (referent of a parameter) ⇒ allowed; `return &mut local` (frame-owned) ⇒ `err`.
scope.outputs: `err` only for a frame-owned local; otherwise allowed.
scope.notes: globals are deliberately absent from the language at this phase; see §5 (functions) when name-resolution scope is formalized.

footgun.statement: No other dangling-reference case is checked — e.g. a local's address smuggled out inside a struct field, or a reference outliving its referent through any more indirect path.
footgun.formal: all dangling cases other than `reference.dangling.return.constraint` are `unspecified` (unchecked).

well-defined.statement: Aliasing is well-defined: the compiler makes no `noalias`/`restrict` assumption that a `&mut` is the only reference to its referent.

program-order.statement: A program's observable behavior is deterministic: operations apply in program order, whether or not two references happen to alias.
program-order.formal: memory operations are ordered as written (no reordering that changes observable behavior); aliasing does not make behavior nondeterministic.

no-exclusivity.statement: Nothing enforces exclusivity: two `&mut` to the same memory, or a `&T` and a `&mut` to the same memory, are both legal; the result is deterministic but almost-certainly-unintended.
no-exclusivity.formal: `&T` forbids writes *through that reference*, not writes by another coexisting `&mut`; the latter is accepted and deterministic.

length-in-type.statement: A fixed-size array's length is part of its type: `f32[3]` and `f32[4]` are distinct types.
length-in-type.inputs: two array types differing only in length.

size-align.statement: `size(T[n]) = n · size(T)`; `align(T[n]) = align(T)`. The length `n` must be ≥ 1 (zero-length arrays are illegal).

copy-semantics.statement: An array is a plain value type: assigning one to another, or passing it by value, copies every element.
copy-semantics.formal: `a = b` (arrays) copies `n` elements; pass-by-value copies the whole array.
copy-semantics.inputs: an array assignment or by-value pass.

mechanism.statement: `arr[index]` is a dedicated language mechanism, not sugar for pointer arithmetic; the compiler computes the element address internally, never exposed to user code.
mechanism.formal: `⟦arr[i]⟧ = base(arr) + i · size(T)` computed by the compiler; no user-visible pointer arithmetic.
mechanism.outputs: the element at the computed address.

type.statement: A subscript index (array or slice) and a range endpoint must be `usz`; the index/endpoint position is a context position of type `usz`, so an integer literal is context-typed to `usz` and a non-`usz` integer expression is a type error.
type.formal: `a[i]` / `s[i]` / `a[i..j]` valid iff `type(i) = usz` (via context typing); else `err`. Index arithmetic is `usz`.
type.inputs: a subscript index or range endpoint.
type.notes: `usz` is the native-word-size unsigned type (previously a `u64` placeholder).

out-of-bounds.statement: Out-of-bounds indexing is not checked at runtime.

size-builtin.statement: `arr.size` gives the array's length as an `usz` — a compile-time constant. It is a read-only builtin, not a declarable field.
size-builtin.formal: `⟦arr.size⟧ = n : usz` (constant, since `n` is part of the type); `.size` is reserved (not a field name).

constant-expression.statement: An array length must be a compile-time constant integer expression evaluating to `k ≥ 1`; a zero, negative, or non-constant (runtime) length is a compile error.
constant-expression.formal: `T[n]` valid iff `n` is a constant expression per `expression.constant-expression` and `⟦n⟧ = k ≥ 1`; else `err`.
constant-expression.outputs: `err` if the length is not a constant `≥ 1`.
constant-expression.notes: the constant-expression domain is `expression.constant-expression` (shared with struct-field defaults).

representation.statement: A slice `T[]` is a non-owning, runtime-sized view — a `{ T*, usz }` pair (16 bytes on 64-bit).

from-array.statement: `&arr` on a fixed-size array produces a slice viewing all of it, reusing `&` but yielding `T[]`, not `&T`.
from-array.formal: `&a ⇒ { ptr = &a[0], len = n } : T[]`; `&mut a ⇒ { ptr = &a[0], len = n } : mut T[]`.
from-array.outputs: a slice (or writable slice) over all elements.

form.statement: `&a` yields a read-only `T[]`; `&mut a` yields a writable `mut T[]`. Neither is address-of-taking in the reference sense.
form.formal: `&a ⇒ T[]`; `&mut a ⇒ mut T[]`; no `&T`/`&mut T` is formed.

take-constraint.statement: `&mut a` requires `a`'s own binding to be `mut`, exactly as for a reference.

writability-in-type.statement: A slice type carries its own writability: `T[]` is read-only, `mut T[]` is writable.

write-readonly.statement: Writing an element through a read-only view is a compile error.

writability-boundary.statement: Because writability is part of the type, it holds across a function boundary: a callee receiving `T[]` cannot write through it regardless of what the caller owns.
writability-boundary.formal: a parameter of type `T[]` admits no writes, independent of call-site ownership.
writability-boundary.inputs: a `T[]` parameter and a write attempt.

rebind.statement: `=` on a slice rebinds it (reassigns the `{ptr, len}`), the same way it rebinds any value; binding mutability governs reassignment, not element writability.
rebind.formal: `s = t` (slices) reassigns `s`'s `{ptr, len}`; allowed iff `binding(s) = mut`.
rebind.inputs: an assignment to a slice binding.

binding-vs-element-mutable.statement: Binding mutability and element writability are separate axes: `let v: mut f32[]` may write `v[0]` but not reassign `v`; `mut v: f32[]` may reassign `v` but not write `v[0]`.
binding-vs-element-mutable.formal: `let v: mut T[]` ⇒ element-write allowed, reassign `err`; `mut v: T[]` ⇒ reassign allowed, element-write `err`.

subslice-preserve-qualifier.statement: Sub-slicing preserves the qualifier: a `mut T[]` sub-slice is `mut T[]`, and a `T[]` sub-slice is `T[]`.
subslice-preserve-qualifier.formal: `type(s[a..b]) = type(s)` (the slice's own mutability carries through).
subslice-preserve-qualifier.outputs: a slice of the same qualifier.

widening.statement: A read-only view can never be widened into a writable one; the reverse is free.
widening.formal: `T[] → mut T[]` ⇒ `err` (no widening); `mut T[] → T[]` ⇒ allowed.

mechanism.statement: `slice[index]` and sub-slicing are dedicated language mechanisms computed by the compiler; a slice's internal base is not a `&T`, cannot be rebound directly, and is never an arithmetic-capable value in user code.
mechanism.formal: `⟦s[i]⟧ = s.ptr + i · size(T)` (compiler-internal); `s.ptr` is not exposed as `&T` and has no user arithmetic.

size-builtin.statement: `slice.size` gives the slice's current length as an `usz` — a load of the slice's length word, the same read-only builtin as `arr.size`.
size-builtin.formal: `⟦s.size⟧ = s.len : usz` (load of the length word).

non-owning.statement: A slice does not own the memory it views; its validity depends on the underlying data outliving it, subject to the dangling-reference risk of §3.6.
non-owning.formal: a slice outliving its backing store ⇒ `unspecified`.
non-owning.inputs: a slice whose backing store is gone.

undefined.statement: A slice is a view, so it cannot be `undefined`-initialized; it comes into existence only by viewing a real array (`&a`/`&mut a`), by sub-slicing, or from a string literal.
undefined.formal: `= undefined` on a slice ⇒ `err`; creation paths are exactly the three listed.
undefined.outputs: `err` for `undefined`; otherwise one of the three creation paths.

range.statement: A range subscript `a[i..j]`/`a[i..=j]` covers the interval per `statement.range.bounds`.

out-of-bounds.statement: A sub-slice range whose bounds fall outside the array/slice, or with `end < start`, is unchecked at runtime (the same risk class as `array.out-of-bounds`).
out-of-bounds.formal: `a[i..j]` with `i ≥ n` or `j > n` or `j < i` ⇒ `unspecified` (no bounds check emitted).
out-of-bounds.inputs: an out-of-bounds or inverted sub-slice range.

of-slice.statement: Both arrays and slices may be sub-sliced; sub-slicing a slice behaves exactly as sub-slicing an array, and the qualifier is preserved.
of-slice.formal: `s[a..b]` on `s : T[]` ⇒ `{ ptr = s.ptr + a·size(T), len = b−a } : T[]`; on `mut T[]` ⇒ `mut T[]`.
of-slice.outputs: a slice of the same qualifier.

syntax.statement: A function declaration is `fn Name(params)`, optionally with `-> ReturnType`; an absent return type means the function returns no value.
syntax.formal: `fn Name(p₁: T₁, …, pₙ: Tₙ) [-> R]`; `R` absent ⇒ no return value.
syntax.outputs: its name, parameter list, and optional return type.

forward-reference.statement: A function may be called before its declaration appears in the file; names are resolved across the whole program.
forward-reference.formal: call-site resolution is independent of textual order; every `fn` name is visible program-wide.
forward-reference.inputs: a call to a function declared later in the file.
forward-reference.outputs: the call resolves to that function.

cross-kind.statement: A symbol name is unique across all kinds: a function, struct, enum, or type may not reuse a name already bound to any other symbol.
cross-kind.formal: two symbols of any kind with the same name ⇒ `err`.
cross-kind.inputs: a declaration whose name collides across kinds.

signature.statement: A function's identity is its name plus the exact types of its parameters in order. Two functions may share a name iff their parameter-type lists differ; the return type does not participate. For a method, the `self` parameter is excluded from the key.
signature.formal: `key(f) = (name(f), ⟨type(p₁), …, type(pₙ)⟩)` over the explicit parameters (excluding a method's `self`); two functions with equal key ⇒ `err`; equal name, different type-list ⇒ overload (allowed).
signature.outputs: `err` iff same name and same explicit parameter-type list.
signature.notes: return type and a method's `self` are both excluded from the key, so `m(&T, x)` and `m(&mut T, x)` are the same overload (duplicate error).

resolve.statement: A call resolves to the unique function whose parameter types exactly match the arguments' *default* (context-free) types; there is no implicit conversion. Zero or multiple matches is a compile error.
resolve.formal: compute `type⁰(aᵢ)` = the context-free type of each argument (a literal → its default width `i32`/`f32`); select the unique `f` with `type⁰(aᵢ) = type(pᵢ)` for all `i`; then apply context typing (`type.context.propagation`) to the args against the selected `pᵢ`. Zero or multiple matches ⇒ `err`.
resolve.inputs: a call site and the candidate overloads.
resolve.outputs: the unique matching function (by default type), or `err`.
resolve.notes: "default type wins": overload selection uses default types, so `Foo(1)` ⇒ `Foo(i32)` even if `Foo(i64)` exists; context typing applies only after the single winner is chosen.

on-all-paths.statement: A function declared `-> R` must `return` a value on every path that reaches its closing brace; reaching the end of a `-> R` body without executing `return` is a compile error.
on-all-paths.formal: for `fn F(...) -> R`, a compile error iff control flow can reach the closing `}` without having executed `return`. Branch-aware: `if`/`else` requires both branches to return; a `while (true)` loop with no reachable `break`/`return` makes the close unreachable (no error).
on-all-paths.outputs: `err` iff the closing brace is reachable on some path with no `return` executed.
on-all-paths.notes: the exact `break`/`continue`/loop interaction is finalized when §10 (while) is extracted; this rule states the reachability semantics.

immutable.statement: A parameter is an immutable binding; it cannot be reassigned.
immutable.inputs: a parameter and an assignment to it.

reassign.statement: Reassigning a parameter is a compile error; mutability is expressed only through the parameter's *type* — a `&mut T` parameter's referent may be written, but the parameter binding itself (the reference) remains immutable and cannot be rebound.

mutable-reference-write.statement: A `&mut` parameter is a reference; writing through it is an explicit dereference.
mutable-reference-write.formal: `*p = v` / `*p += v` (with `p : &mut T`) writes the referent.
mutable-reference-write.inputs: a `&mut` parameter and a write through it.

pass-by-value.statement: A value-type argument (primitive, struct, array) is passed by value: the argument is copied into the parameter's storage. (Large values are passed by reference explicitly via `&`/`&mut`.)
pass-by-value.formal: passing `arg : T` (value type) to `p : T` copies `arg` into `p`; `p` is a distinct value.
pass-by-value.inputs: a value-type argument and its parameter.

no-value.statement: A function without a return type produces no value; a call to it may appear only as a statement, and using it where a value is expected is a compile error.
no-value.formal: `F()` with no return type ⇒ no value; `… = F()` / `F()` in an expression ⇒ `err`.
no-value.inputs: a call to a void function.

bare-return.statement: In a function without a return type, a bare `return;` may optionally exit the body early and return to the caller; falling off the closing brace also returns.
bare-return.formal: `return;` in a void body transfers control to the caller; reaching the closing `}` does likewise.
bare-return.notes: converse: a bare `return;` in a `-> R` function is an error (no value returned).

return-value.statement: `return e;` in a function with no return type is a compile error.
return-value.inputs: a value-return in a void function.

definition.statement: A function whose first parameter is a reference to its own struct type (`&Type` or `&mut Type`) is a method.
definition.formal: `is_method(f) ⇔ type(first param of f) ∈ {&S, &mut S}` for the struct `S` that namespaces `f`.

self-convention.statement: `self` is a naming convention, not a keyword; method-ness is determined by the first parameter's *type*, not its name.
self-convention.formal: the first parameter may be named anything; a `&S`/`&mut S` first parameter makes it a method regardless of the name.
self-convention.outputs: method-ness independent of the parameter's name.

consistency.statement: All overloads of a namespaced name must agree on method-ness: every overload has a `self` parameter, or none do. Mixing method and non-method overloads under one name is a compile error.
consistency.formal: for a name `m` namespaced to `S`, either `∀ i: is_method(mᵢ)` or `∀ i: ¬is_method(mᵢ)`; a mix ⇒ `err`.
consistency.inputs: the overloads of a namespaced name.
consistency.outputs: `err` if method-ness is mixed across overloads.

call-sugar.statement: Calling a method on a value `v.m(args)` desugars to `S.m(&v, args)` (or `S.m(&mut v, args)` for a `&mut` self).
call-sugar.formal: `v.m(a) ≡ S.m(&v, a)` when self is `&S`; `v.m(a) ≡ S.m(&mut v, a)` when self is `&mut S`.
call-sugar.inputs: a method call on a value.
call-sugar.notes: the reference's example shows `&my_transform` for a `&mut` self; the `&mut` form is the correct desugaring (see `function.method.mutable-self-constraint`).

mutable-self-constraint.statement: `&mut Type` self-parameters require the instance's own binding to be `mut`.
mutable-self-constraint.formal: `v.m(a)` with `m`'s first param `&mut S` valid iff `binding(v) = mut`, else `err`.
mutable-self-constraint.inputs: a method call whose self parameter is `&mut`.

arrow-call.statement: Calling a method on a reference uses `->`: where `r: &mut Transform`, `r->Translate(1, 1)` is `Transform.Translate(r, 1, 1)` — it passes the reference itself, not `&r`.
arrow-call.inputs: a method call on a reference.

namespaced-call.statement: A function declared without a leading self-parameter is namespaced to the type but is not a method, and is called as `S.name(args)`.
namespaced-call.formal: non-method namespaced functions are called `S.f(args)`, never `v.f(args)`.

entry.statement: `main` is the program's entry point. Its signature is `fn main(args: byte[][]) -> i32` — one parameter, a read-only `byte[][]` of program arguments, and an `i32` return whose value is the program's observable result.
entry.formal: execution begins by calling `main`; `args : byte[][]`; `⟦main(args)⟧ : i32` is the program's observable result.
entry.notes: the source of `args`' backing storage (operating-system arguments) and the mapping of the `i32` to a process exit code are runtime-spec concerns, not language rules.

unique.statement: A program has exactly one `main`; zero or more than one is a compile error.
unique.outputs: `err` if there is not exactly one `main`.

body.statement: A struct's body lists its fields, followed by the signatures of any functions namespaced onto the type.
body.formal: `struct S { f₁: T₁; …; fn m(…) -> …; … }` — fields first, then function signatures.
body.outputs: its field list and namespaced-function signature list.

complete.statement: The signature list is the struct's complete interface — a function may be namespaced onto a type only if its signature is declared in the struct body.
complete.formal: `fn S.m(…)` (implementation) valid iff `m`'s signature is declared in `S`'s body; else `err`.
complete.outputs: `err` if its signature is not declared in the struct.

unique-names.statement: Struct field names must be unique within the struct.
unique-names.formal: two fields with the same name in one struct ⇒ `err`.
unique-names.inputs: a struct with duplicate field names.

recursion.statement: A struct may not contain itself transitively *by value* (its size would be non-finite); a field of reference type (`&S`, `&mut S`) is legal and is not recursion, since a reference is a pointer, not a nested value.
recursion.formal: `S` is ill-formed iff `S` transitively contains `S` through value-typed fields (making `size(S)` an ungrounded recurrence); a `&S` field contributes `size(&S) = 8`, not `size(S)`, so it is legal.
recursion.inputs: a struct with a (transitive) self-referential field.
recursion.outputs: `err` for by-value self-containment; legal for reference fields.

semantics.statement: A field may declare a default value, used when the field is otherwise uninitialized.
semantics.formal: `f: T = d` declares `d` as the field's default, used per `variable.initialization.defaulted.semantics`.
semantics.inputs: a field declaration with a default.

constant.statement: A field default must be a compile-time constant expression.
constant.formal: `f: T = d` valid iff `d` is a constant expression per `expression.constant-expression`; else `err`.

value-only.statement: A default may appear only on value fields; a reference-typed field cannot declare a default.
value-only.inputs: a reference-typed field with a default.

qualified.statement: Implementations are written separately, qualified with the struct's name, and may appear anywhere in the program.
qualified.formal: `fn S.m(…) -> R { … }` defines `m` for `S`; position/order in the file is unconstrained.

order.statement: Struct fields are laid out in declaration order.

offset.statement: Each field is placed at its natural alignment: the first field at offset 0; each subsequent field at the first offset ≥ (previous field's offset + its size) that is a multiple of the field's alignment, inserting padding as needed.

align.statement: A struct's alignment is the largest of its fields' alignments; an empty struct has alignment 1.
align.formal: `align(S) = max over fields f of align(type(f))`; `align(S) = 1` if `fields(S) = ∅`.

size.statement: A struct's size is rounded up to a multiple of its alignment; an empty struct has size 1.

empty.statement: A zero-field struct is legal and has size 1 and alignment 1.
empty.notes: chosen for distinct addresses, well-behaved arrays (`Marker[3]` ⇒ size 3), and consistency with the zero-length-array rejection (`gap.slice.2`).

padding.statement: Padding bytes inserted for alignment are zeroed on default-initialization (form a); `undefined`-initialization leaves them unspecified.
padding.formal: default-init (form a) zeroes the entire value including padding (a single memset over `size(S)`); `undefined`-init ⇒ padding `unspecified`.
padding.outputs: zeroed padding on default-init; unspecified padding on `undefined`-init.

endian.statement: All multi-byte values are stored little-endian: the least-significant byte at the lowest address.
endian.formal: for a value of width `N` bytes, byte `i` (0 = LSB) is at `address + i`; little-endian order throughout.

representation.statement: An enum holds exactly one variant; in memory it is a tag at offset 0, then padding, then the payload area; the enum's alignment is the max of the tag's and the largest variant's alignments; its size is rounded up to that alignment.
representation.formal: `offset(tag) = 0`; `size(tag) = size(TagType)`; `align(payload) = maxᵥ align(V)`, `size(payload) = maxᵥ size(V)`; `offset(payload) = align_up(size(TagType), align(payload))`; `align(E) = max(align(TagType), align(payload))`; `size(E) = align_up(offset(payload) + size(payload), align(E))`.
representation.notes: `align(E) = max(tag, largest variant)` fixes the prose's omission of the tag's alignment (a latent bug when the tag is wider than the payload).

syntax.statement: An enum is declared `enum Name: TagType { V₁, V₂(params), … }`.
syntax.outputs: its name, tag type, and variants.

mandatory.statement: The tag type is mandatory and explicit; there is no auto-inference from variant count.
mandatory.inputs: an enum declaration lacking a tag type.

type.statement: The tag type must be a fixed-width unsigned integer (`u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u64`); the number of variants must be representable in the tag's width. `usz` is excluded to keep enum layout ABI-stable across architectures.
type.inputs: an enum tag type and its variant count.
type.outputs: `err` if the tag type is not a fixed-width unsigned integer, or if the variant count overflows the tag width.
type.notes: `usz` is excluded: a native-width tag would make enum size/align vary by target, breaking ABI stability.

min-one.statement: An enum must declare at least one variant; a zero-variant (uninhabited) enum is a compile error.
min-one.inputs: an enum declaration with no variants.

no-data.statement: A variant with no data omits the parameter list: `NoOp,` not `NoOp(),`.
no-data.formal: a data-less variant is written without `()`; `NoOp()` ⇒ `err`.

payload-syntax.statement: Variant payloads are declared using the same syntax as function parameter lists.
payload-syntax.formal: `V(p₁: T₁, …, pₙ: Tₙ)` mirrors function parameter syntax.

field-names.statement: Variant payload fields must be named and unique within the variant; construction and destructuring remain positional.
field-names.formal: every payload field is `name: T` (name required); two fields with the same name in one variant ⇒ `err`; use is positional.
field-names.outputs: `err` if a field is unnamed or a name repeats within the variant.

reference-payload.statement: A variant may hold a reference to a larger payload instead of the payload inline.

qualified.statement: A value is constructed by qualifying the variant name with its enum, passing field values positionally in declared order.

unit-variant.statement: A data-less variant is constructed without parentheses: `Event.NoOp`.
unit-variant.outputs: an enum value with no payload.

manual.statement: Boxing is manual — the language never boxes a variant automatically.
manual.formal: no implicit heap allocation for any variant.

dangling.statement: A reference-holding variant is subject to the same dangling risk as any other reference.
dangling.formal: a reference-payload variant outliving its referent ⇒ `unspecified`.
dangling.inputs: a reference-payload variant whose referent is gone.

expression.formal: `match (e) { arms }` yields a value when used as an expression.

enum.statement: The subject of `match` must be an enum; other discrete representable values use `switch` (§8).
enum.formal: `match (e)` valid iff `type(e)` is an enum; else `err`.

single-expression.statement: A single-expression arm's value is that expression.

block-yield.statement: A block-bodied arm produces its value via an explicit `yield expr;`, which exits the block immediately, the same way `return` exits a function.
block-yield.formal: `Pat => { …; yield e; … }` ⇒ arm value = `⟦e⟧`; `yield` exits the block immediately.
block-yield.notes: `yield` is a statement whose full control-flow rules (§8–§11) are deferred; this rule states only its match-arm consequence.

discarded-no-yield.statement: When a match's result is discarded, block-bodied arms need not `yield` and run as an ordinary statement sequence.
discarded-no-yield.formal: in statement position, `yield` is optional in block arms.
discarded-no-yield.inputs: a discarded match with block arms.

exhaustive.statement: `match` must handle every variant of the enum being matched.
exhaustive.formal: the arm patterns must cover all variants of `type(e)`; else `err` (unless a final `else` is present).
exhaustive.outputs: `err` if a variant is unhandled and no `else`.

else-arm.statement: `else` covers the remaining variants and must be the final arm; an arm after `else` is a compile error (unreachable).
else-arm.formal: `else => e` matches any variant not matched earlier; `else` must be the last arm — an arm following `else` ⇒ `err`.
else-arm.inputs: an `else` arm and any arm following it.
else-arm.outputs: covers the remainder; `err` if an arm follows `else`.

positional.statement: Payload destructuring is positional, matching the variant's declared field order; a field that isn't needed can be bound and left unused.
positional.formal: `V(p₁, …, pₙ)` binds each payload field positionally to `pᵢ`; unused bindings are allowed.

condition-bool.statement: The condition of `if` and `while` must be `bool`; no implicit conversion from any other type.

braces-optional.statement: Braces are optional; without braces, exactly one statement follows — a sequence of statements requires `{ }`.
braces-optional.formal: a body is either `{ stmt* }` or a single statement (no braces).

no-fallthrough.statement: The arms of `match` and `switch` are checked in order, and no fallthrough occurs — exactly one arm's expression is evaluated.
no-fallthrough.formal: arms are tested top-to-bottom; the first matching arm is chosen; no fallthrough.

same-type.statement: When `match`/`switch`/`if` is used as an expression, every arm/branch must produce a value of the same type.

subject.statement: `switch` matches a value against primitive literals, multiple discrete values, or ranges; the subject must be an integer (`i*`/`u*`/`isz`/`usz`) or `byte` — not `bool`, not floats.
subject.formal: `switch (e)` valid iff `type(e) ∈ {i8..i64, u8..u64, isz, usz, byte}`; else `err`.
subject.outputs: `err` unless the subject is an integer or `byte`.
subject.notes: `isz`/`usz` are included (they are integers); unlike enum tags, `switch` has no layout, so no ABI concern.

arm.statement: An arm has the form `case => result`, where the result is a single expression or a block with `yield` (same as `match`).

multi-value.statement: An arm may list multiple comma-separated values, matching if the subject equals any of them.
multi-value.formal: `v₁, v₂, …, vₙ => e` matches when `e == vᵢ` for some `i`.

case-literal.statement: A case cites one or more literals, not expressions.
case-literal.formal: a case value is a literal (or a range of literals); a non-literal case ⇒ `err`.
case-literal.outputs: `err` if the case is not a literal.

range.statement: A range case `a..b`/`a..=b` matches the subject if it falls within the interval (bounds per `statement.range.bounds`).

range-literal.statement: A range case's endpoints are literals, not expressions.
range-literal.formal: `a..b`/`a..=b` in a case: `a` and `b` are literals; a non-literal endpoint ⇒ `err`.
range-literal.outputs: `err` if an endpoint is not a literal.

mix.statement: A case may mix single values and ranges freely; each is checked as its own match.
mix.formal: `v₁, a..b, v₂, … => e` — each entry is an independent match.

else-required.statement: A final `else` arm is mandatory; omitting it is a compile error.

subject-literal-form.statement: The subject's type determines the literal form its cases are written in: an integer subject switches on integer literals, a `byte` subject on `byte` literals.
subject-literal-form.formal: `type(subject)` selects the case literal form (integer vs `byte`).
subject-literal-form.inputs: a switch subject and its cases.

expression.statement: `switch` is an expression, with the same single-expression/`yield` arm rules as `match`.
expression.formal: `switch (e) { arms }` yields a value when used as an expression.

endpoint-form.statement: Range endpoints are literals in a `switch` case (a closed compile-time table), but in a `for` loop or a subscript they may be arbitrary expressions — runtime variables, literals, or a mix.
endpoint-form.formal: `switch` case range: endpoints are literals (`statement.switch.range-literal`); `for`/subscript range: endpoints are expressions (typed `usz`, per `type.context.positions`).
endpoint-form.outputs: the permitted endpoint form (literal vs expression).

bounds.statement: A range `a..b` is exclusive of `b`; `a..=b` is inclusive of `b`. These are the only two range forms, and they appear wherever a range does.

endpoint-agree.statement: The two endpoints of a range must have the same type; a mismatch is a compile error (no implicit conversion).
endpoint-agree.notes: switch endpoints (literals, context-typed) and subscript endpoints (`usz`) agree by construction; this constraint chiefly governs `for`-range endpoints.

not-a-value.statement: A range is not a value: `a..b`/`a..=b` may appear in exactly three positions — a `switch` case, after `in` in a `for`, and as a subscript. A range cannot be bound, stored, passed, or returned (there is no range type).
not-a-value.formal: a range in any other position ⇒ `err`.
not-a-value.outputs: `err` unless in one of the three positions.

expression.statement: `if` is an expression; the single-line form also serves as the ternary (no separate `? :` operator).
expression.formal: `if (c) a else b` yields a value when used as an expression.

single-statement-value.statement: A single-statement branch's value is that statement's expression.

block-yield.statement: A block-bodied branch produces its value via an explicit `yield expr;`, the same as `match`/`switch`.

branch-value.statement: When `if` is used as an expression, each branch must produce a value, checked independently: a block branch via `yield expr;`, and a single-statement branch must be an expression (a value-less statement like `while`/`for`/`return`/`break`/`continue` is a compile error). Block and single-statement branches may be mixed.
branch-value.formal: for `if` in expression position, every branch must produce a value; a single-statement branch whose statement is value-less ⇒ `err`.
branch-value.outputs: `err` if any branch produces no value.

else-required.statement: When used as an expression, a final `else` is mandatory — there is no default value for an uncovered path.

dangling-else.statement: With braces optional, a bare `else` following nested unbraced `if`s attaches to the nearest preceding `if` that doesn't already have one (C's rule).
dangling-else.formal: `else` binds to the innermost preceding `if` without an `else`.

statement.statement: `while` is a statement, not an expression — its body may execute zero times, so no value can be guaranteed to come out of it.

break.statement: `break` exits the innermost enclosing loop immediately.
break.formal: `break;` transfers control to just after the loop body.

continue.statement: `continue` skips to the next condition check (for `while`), advancing the index (for `for`).
continue.formal: `continue;` jumps to the loop's next iteration.
continue.outputs: control skips to the next iteration.

loop-only.statement: `break`/`continue` are valid only inside a loop body; using either outside one is a compile error.

innermost.statement: `break`/`continue` always affect the innermost enclosing loop — there is no labeled break/continue.
innermost.formal: a `break`/`continue` targets the innermost enclosing loop only.

in-arm.statement: `break`/`continue` may appear inside a block-bodied arm of a `match`/`switch`/`if` nested in a loop; they are bound by the innermost enclosing loop, not by the arm.
in-arm.formal: `break`/`continue` in an arm bind to the enclosing loop.
in-arm.inputs: a `break`/`continue` in an arm nested in a loop.

no-yield.statement: If an arm must produce a value (its enclosing `match`/`switch`/`if` is an expression), reaching a bare `break`/`continue` with no `yield` is a compile error.
no-yield.formal: bare `break`/`continue` in a value-producing arm ⇒ `err`; use `break yield x;`. When the construct's value is discarded, bare `break`/`continue` are unrestricted.
no-yield.inputs: a bare `break`/`continue` in a value-producing arm.

infinite-loop.statement: An infinite loop is written `while (true) { … }`; there is no separate `loop` keyword.

innermost.statement: `yield` always produces a value for the innermost enclosing expression — the `match`, `switch`, or `if` it appears in — never for the loop, which is a statement.
innermost.outputs: produces the value for that construct.

requires-expression.statement: `yield` requires an enclosing `match`/`switch`/`if` expression; a `yield` with no such enclosing expression (e.g. directly in a function or loop body) is a compile error.
requires-expression.formal: `yield e;` valid iff within the body of a `match`/`switch`/`if`; else `err`.

semantics.statement: `break yield x;` produces `x` for the enclosing expression, then exits the loop.
semantics.formal: `break yield x;` ⇒ the enclosing `match`/`switch`/`if` yields `⟦x⟧`, then control exits the loop.

scope.statement: `break yield`/`continue yield` are valid only where the innermost enclosing expression construct lies inside the loop being left — there must be something for the value to be produced for.
scope.formal: `break yield x;`/`continue yield x;` valid iff an enclosing `match`/`switch`/`if` is inside the loop; else `err`.
scope.outputs: `err` if no enclosing expression construct is in the loop.

continue-yield.statement: `continue yield x;` produces `x` for the enclosing expression, then abandons the iteration.
continue-yield.formal: `continue yield x;` ⇒ the enclosing expression yields `⟦x⟧`, then the iteration is abandoned.
continue-yield.notes: `continue yield` is legal but never useful (the value is discarded when the iteration is abandoned).

statement.statement: `for` is a statement, not an expression — the iterated sequence may be empty, so no value can be guaranteed to come out of it.

iterable.statement: The iterated sequence is a range, a slice, or a fixed-size array.
iterable.formal: `for (v in seq)` where `seq` is a range, `T[]`, or `T[n]`.

range-iter.statement: Iterating a range binds the loop variable to each integer from `a` to `b`, inclusive or exclusive per `statement.range.bounds`; the loop variable's type is the endpoints' common type (default `i32` for unsuffixed literals).
range-iter.formal: `for (i in a..b)` ⇒ `i = a, a+1, …, b-1`, with `type(i) = type(a) = type(b)`; `for (i in a..=b)` ⇒ `i = a, …, b`.
range-iter.outputs: the loop variable takes each integer in the range, typed as the endpoints.

slice-array-iter.statement: Iterating a slice or array binds the loop variable to each element, in order from the first to the last.
slice-array-iter.formal: `for (v in s)` ⇒ `v = s[0], s[1], …, s[n-1]` (a value copy per element).
slice-array-iter.outputs: the loop variable takes each element.

loop-variable.statement: The loop variable is a per-iteration binding, not a reference, and is immutable regardless of the iterated value's own binding.
loop-variable.formal: `for (v in …)` ⇒ `v` is a fresh immutable binding each iteration (a value copy, not a view).

loop-variable-reassign.statement: Reassigning the loop variable inside the body is a compile error; mutating an element requires writing to the collection by index or through a writable slice.
loop-variable-reassign.inputs: an assignment to the loop variable.

desugar.statement: `for` is sugar for an indexed `while` (step the index, compare against the end, read the current element); `break`/`continue`/nesting/innermost-binding are exactly §10's.
desugar.formal: `for (v in a..b) { B }` ≡ an indexed `while` over the range; `for (v in s)` ≡ an indexed `while` over `0..s.size`.

type.statement: A string literal initializes a `byte[]` slice (a read-only view of `.rodata`), not a distinct type; it may also initialize a fixed `byte[n]` array (see `string.literal.to-array`).
type.formal: `type("…") = byte[]` (a slice view); `byte[n] = "…"` copies the bytes into an array.
type.outputs: a `byte[]` slice, or an initialized `byte[n]` array.

to-array.statement: A string literal may initialize a fixed `byte[n]` array by copying its UTF-8 bytes from `.rodata`; the UTF-8 byte count must fit in `n`, checked **at compile time** (the literal's length is a constant), else a compile error. Any remaining elements are default-initialized (zeroed).
to-array.formal: `byte[n] = "…"` valid iff `len(utf8("…")) ≤ n` — a compile-time check (no runtime bounds check); else `err`. Bytes fill `[0, len)`, the rest are zeroed.
to-array.inputs: a string literal initializing a `byte[n]` array.
to-array.outputs: the array with the string's bytes copied in; `err` if it doesn't fit.

rodata.statement: A string literal's bytes are placed in read-only static storage (`.rodata`); the literal is a view of those bytes.
rodata.formal: the literal's bytes live in `.rodata`; the `byte[]` value is `{ ptr = &rodata, len = n }`.
rodata.outputs: a slice viewing read-only static bytes.

no-alloc.statement: A string literal never allocates; there is no owning or growable string type (an owning string, if any, is a later phase).
no-alloc.formal: no heap allocation for a literal; no owning-string type exists.

no-null.statement: A string literal stores exactly its contents — there is no trailing null terminator; the length is carried in the slice.
no-null.formal: `len("…") = n` (byte count of the contents); no implicit `\0` appended.
no-null.outputs: the exact byte contents with no terminator.

escapes.statement: String literals support the same escape sequences as `byte` literals: `\0 \n \r \t \\ \" \'`. There is no raw-literal form.
escapes.formal: escapes(string) = escapes(byte) per `type.byte.literal.escapes`; no raw-literal syntax.

utf8-source.statement: A string literal's source characters are UTF-8; the full 1–4-byte codepoint range is valid (`"é"`, `"😀"`), and the compiler decodes the source as UTF-8 and emits the UTF-8 bytes.
utf8-source.formal: a string literal may contain any UTF-8 codepoint; `"é"` ⇒ bytes `0xC3 0xA9`.
utf8-source.inputs: a string literal with UTF-8 source characters.

utf8.statement: The compiler verifies that a string literal is valid UTF-8 and emits its UTF-8 bytes; an invalid UTF-8 sequence is a compile error.
utf8.formal: each literal is validated as UTF-8 at compile time; invalid ⇒ `err`.

readonly.statement: A string literal always decays to a read-only `byte[]` view; it is never `&mut`-taken, so it can never yield a writable view, and writing through it is a compile error.
readonly.formal: a literal is a read-only `byte[]`; `&mut "…"` ⇒ `err`; writing through the view ⇒ `err` (per `slice.write-readonly`).
readonly.inputs: a string literal and any write attempt.

ops.statement: The built-in operations on a string are exactly §4's slice operations and nothing more: `.size` (length in bytes), `s[i]` (the `byte` at `i`), and `s[a..b]` (a `byte[]` sub-slice). No concatenation, formatting, or search exists.
ops.outputs: the slice operation's result; other ops are `err`.

bytes-not-chars.statement: A string is a `byte[]`, so `.size`, indexing, and sub-slicing count *bytes*, not characters; on multibyte UTF-8 these misalign (e.g. `"é".size` is 2, and `s[1..2]` can split a codepoint). This is expected behavior, not a footgun — character-level handling is a later string-object concern.
bytes-not-chars.formal: `.size`/`[i]`/`[a..b]` operate on byte positions; no character semantics are provided.
bytes-not-chars.inputs: a string and a byte-position operation.
bytes-not-chars.outputs: byte-based results (may split a UTF-8 sequence).
